summary: An excerpt from a novel (Book 12, part 23) following Lexy, a practical young woman who sees herself as unromantic and is carrying out a task for her friend Caroline Enderby. On a train she notices a tall, distinguished, dark and haughty stranger, whom she finds less appealing than the blue-eyed Mr. Houseman. At the rainy, dark station of Wyngate, the stranger takes the only taxi, and Lexy's request to the driver for a return trip is interrupted when the stranger leaps out and apologizes. A sentence about Stuart viewing Monet's 'Impression, Sunrise' in 2013 appears out of place in the text and does not connect to the story.
one_line: Lexy, a self-declared unromantic young woman, clashes with a dark, haughty stranger over a solitary taxi at the rainy station of Wyngate.
key_facts: Lexy had no coquetry in her honest heart and viewed her friends' little flirtations with distaste and wonder.
Lexy said "I'm not romantic!" more than once and believed it.
Lexy regarded her present mission as a matter-of-course thing she was in honor bound to do for her friend Caroline Enderby.
On the train Lexy saw a very tall, slenderly and strongly built young man dressed with fastidious perfection and an air of marked distinction.
Lexy preferred the blue-eyed Mr. Houseman's blunt, sunburned face to the dark and haughty face of the stranger.
Lexy was reading a detective story on the train, which she enjoyed uncritically and absorbedly.
Lexy caught the stranger's eye more than once as she looked up at the train's stations.
The stranger got out at Wyngate with Lexy shortly after five o'clock on a rainy afternoon when it was already dark.
At Wyngate a solitary taxi was drawn up beside the platform, and the stranger reached it before Lexy and spoke to the driver.
No other taxi, vehicle, or lights were visible at Wyngate except those of the station.
The stranger jumped into the cab and slammed the door, and Lexy called out, "Driver! Will you please come back for me?"
Before the driver could answer, the stranger sprang out of the cab and said, "I beg your pardon!"
The text includes an out-of-place sentence stating that in 2013 Stuart saw the original 'Impression, Sunrise' painting up close after waiting in line for hours.
